lessonTitle: Intestinal Obstruction and Hernia: Recognition, Strangulation and Management

blocks.text: An 81-year-old woman has vomited three times since morning and has not passed wind. On examination there is a firm, tender, irreducible lump just below and lateral to the pubic tubercle that the family had never noticed. A lump the size of a grape can strangle a loop of bowel within hours, which is why every obstructed patient needs every hernial orifice examined.

blocks.markdown: **Intestinal obstruction** is failure of aboral passage of intestinal contents. It is *mechanical* when something blocks the lumen (adhesions, hernia, tumour, volvulus, stricture, gallstone, faecal impaction) and *functional* (ileus or pseudo-obstruction) when peristalsis fails without a blockage. Proximal to the block, bowel and fluid accumulate; the gut wall oedematises, absorption falls and secretion rises, so large volumes of fluid are sequestered in the lumen. The patient becomes dehydrated, with electrolyte disturbance, and rising intraluminal pressure impairs venous return and then arterial inflow.

blocks.title: Closed loop, strangulation and a hernia
blocks.text: A closed-loop obstruction has a blockage at both ends of a bowel segment, so pressure rises rapidly and the segment may perforate or infarct. Strangulation is loss of blood supply to the obstructed bowel. A hernia is protrusion of a viscus or part of it through a defect in the wall that normally contains it; it is irreducible when it cannot be returned, obstructed when the lumen is blocked, and strangulated when its blood supply is compromised.

blocks.markdown: **The four cardinal features** are colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation (no faeces or flatus). Their relative prominence depends on the level. In high small-bowel obstruction, vomiting is early and profuse and distension is minimal. In distal small-bowel obstruction, pain, distension and later faeculent vomiting appear. In large-bowel obstruction, distension and constipation dominate, vomiting is late, and the history may include change in bowel habit or weight loss from a tumour.

blocks.caption: Small-bowel versus large-bowel obstruction
rows: Adhesions, hernia, then tumour or Crohn stricture
Central loops with valvulae conniventes crossing the whole width
Peripheral, haustra not crossing the whole width
Colon above 6 cm; caecum above 9 cm

blocks.title: Reading an abdominal radiograph and CT
blocks.prompt: A 66-year-old man with a previous right hemicolectomy presents with colicky pain, vomiting and distension. The supine abdominal film shows central, dilated loops with lines that cross the full width of the bowel, and a collapsed colon. A CT shows a transition point in the right iliac fossa without a mass. Interpret.

steps.text: Lines crossing the full width are valvulae conniventes, found in jejunum and proximal ileum; their position and pattern point to small bowel.
Dilated central loops with a collapsed colon means the blockage lies above the ileocaecal valve and the large bowel is not distended.
A transition point with no mass, in a patient with previous abdominal surgery, is typical of an adhesional band.
The next question is whether there is any sign of strangulation, such as bowel wall thickening, free fluid, mesenteric congestion or lack of mural enhancement.

blocks.answer: Small-bowel obstruction, most likely adhesional; CT also screens for strangulation and guides conservative versus operative management.

blocks.markdown: **Hernias.** Inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral hernias lie below and lateral to it, passing through the femoral canal beneath the inguinal ligament. A femoral hernia has a narrow, rigid neck and is relatively more common in older women; it carries the highest risk of strangulation and is therefore repaired urgently once identified, even when it is reducible. In a Richter-type hernia only part of the bowel wall is trapped, so there may be strangulation without obstruction.

blocks.title: Strangulation is a surgical emergency
blocks.text: Suspect strangulation when pain becomes constant rather than colicky, with fever, tachycardia, raised lactate, localised peritonism, or a hernia that is tense, tender, red and irreducible. Delay leads to bowel infarction, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis and resection with stoma; mortality rises with delay.

blocks.caption: Complications of an untreated irreducible hernia
rows: Contents cannot be pushed back, no obstruction yet
Lump does not reduce, otherwise well
Venous then arterial occlusion causes ischaemia
Constant pain, tender red lump, fever, raised lactate
Faecal contamination of the sac or peritoneum

blocks.title: Replacing fluid in obstruction
blocks.prompt: A 70 kg adult with small-bowel obstruction needs nasogastric decompression. In 24 hours the NG tube drains 1.8 L. Use maintenance water of 25 mL/kg/day and replace measured NG losses volume for volume, using crystalloid with potassium added per electrolyte results. Calculate the 24-hour prescription and the infusion rate.

steps.text: Maintenance water: 25 mL/kg/day multiplied by weight.
Add replacement of measured NG losses.
Divide by 24 hours for the average rate.

blocks.answer: About 3.55 L over 24 h (about 148 mL/h), reviewed regularly against urine output, electrolytes and clinical state.

items: Resuscitate: intravenous fluids, correct electrolytes, catheter for urine output.
Decompress: nasogastric tube on free drainage ('drip and suck'), nil by mouth.
Image: CT is usually the best test to find cause and exclude strangulation; water-soluble contrast can be both diagnostic and therapeutic in adhesional small-bowel obstruction.
Operate promptly for peritonitis, suspected strangulation, closed-loop obstruction, hernia complications, or failure of conservative treatment.
Large-bowel obstruction from cancer: surgical resection with or without a stoma, or colonic stenting as a bridge or palliation in selected patients.

blocks.title: Conservative versus operative
blocks.text: Selected patients with adhesional small-bowel obstruction and no signs of strangulation are managed conservatively for a defined period (commonly a few days) with serial examination. Hernia-related obstruction, peritonitis, closed-loop obstruction, and obstruction with ischaemia are not suitable for conservative management and require urgent surgery.

points: Small-bowel obstruction: early vomiting, central dilated loops with valvulae conniventes; large-bowel: late vomiting, marked distension, peripheral haustral colon.
Always examine all hernial orifices; a femoral hernia has the highest strangulation risk and needs urgent repair.
Strangulation presents with constant pain, fever, raised lactate and a tense tender irreducible lump, and needs emergency surgery.
Initial management is fluids, nasogastric decompression and imaging; operate early for strangulation, peritonitis or failure to settle.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has had profuse early vomiting, only mild distension and colicky pain. Which level of obstruction is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: early profuse vomiting with little distension is characteristic.
distractorRationale.b: Sigmoid obstruction presents with marked distension and late vomiting.
distractorRationale.c: Rectal obstruction is dominated by constipation and late features.
distractorRationale.d: Caecal or right colon obstruction gives distension, not early profuse vomiting.

questions.explanation: The higher the obstruction, the earlier and more profuse the vomiting and the less the distension, because there is little bowel to distend above the block. Distal and large-bowel obstruction accumulate gas and fluid, giving distension with late vomiting.

questions.stem: A supine abdominal radiograph shows gas in a peripheral, dilated colon with haustral markings that do not cross the full width of the bowel; the caecum measures 11 cm. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.text: This is large-bowel obstruction and the caecal calibre warns of impending perforation
This is a normal film because the caecum may reach 11 cm
This is small-bowel obstruction because valvulae conniventes are seen
This shows gas under the diaphragm

questions.correctOptionText: This is large-bowel obstruction and the caecal calibre warns of impending perforation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: peripheral position with haustra and a caecum above 9 cm indicates large-bowel obstruction with risk of perforation.
distractorRationale.b: Caecal diameter above 9 cm is abnormal.
distractorRationale.c: Valvulae conniventes cross the full width and are central, which is not described here.
distractorRationale.d: Nothing in the description suggests free gas.

questions.explanation: Haustral folds that do not cross the whole width and peripheral gas indicate colon rather than small bowel. A caecal diameter above about 9 cm indicates risk of caecal perforation, especially with a competent ileocaecal valve forming a closed loop.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman has a tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with vomiting. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
distractorRationale.b: An inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the tubercle.
distractorRationale.c: Lymphadenopathy would not cause vomiting and obstruction.
distractorRationale.d: A saphena varix is soft and disappears on lying flat.

questions.explanation: The femoral canal lies below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and femoral hernias are more frequent in older women. Their narrow neck makes strangulation common, so this patient needs urgent surgical assessment.

questions.stem: Which finding in a patient with a known inguinal hernia most strongly suggests strangulation?

options.text: Constant pain with a tense, tender, red, irreducible lump and fever
A soft lump that reduces on lying flat
A lump with a cough impulse and no tenderness
Dragging discomfort at the end of the day

questions.correctOptionText: Constant pain with a tense, tender, red, irreducible lump and fever

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these are signs of ischaemia and inflammation.
distractorRationale.c: A cough impulse alone indicates an uncomplicated hernia.
distractorRationale.d: Dragging discomfort is a typical symptom of an uncomplicated hernia.

questions.explanation: Strangulation produces ischaemic bowel, so pain becomes constant and the lump tense, tender, discoloured and irreducible, often with systemic signs. Uncomplicated hernias are reducible and painless or mildly aching.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman, three years after a hysterectomy, has small-bowel obstruction on CT with a transition point but no bowel wall thickening or free fluid. She is haemodynamically stable with a soft abdomen. Which management is most appropriate?

options.text: Nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluids, water-soluble contrast and serial review, with surgery if she deteriorates or fails to resolve

questions.correctOptionText: Nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluids, water-soluble contrast and serial review, with surgery if she deteriorates or fails to resolve

distractorRationale.a: Correct: adhesional obstruction without strangulation features is trial-of-conservative-care territory.
distractorRationale.b: Not required when there are no signs of strangulation.
distractorRationale.c: Laxatives are inappropriate in mechanical obstruction.
distractorRationale.d: Prokinetics risk perforation in mechanical obstruction.

questions.explanation: Stable patients with adhesional obstruction and no CT or clinical features of ischaemia are managed with decompression, fluids and a trial of water-soluble contrast, with regular reassessment. Failure to progress or any sign of strangulation triggers surgery.

questions.stem: A 60 kg patient with small-bowel obstruction receives maintenance water of 25 mL/kg/day plus volume-for-volume replacement of nasogastric losses. Over 24 hours the NG tube drains 2.1 L. What total fluid volume, in mL, should be prescribed for 24 hours?
questions.explanation: Maintenance water is 25 x 60 = 1500 mL and NG losses are 2100 mL, giving 1500 + 2100 = 3600 mL. In practice the prescription is reviewed frequently against urine output and electrolytes.

questions.stem: An 80 kg patient with adhesional small-bowel obstruction is to receive maintenance water of 25 mL/kg/day plus volume-for-volume replacement of measured losses, delivered at a constant rate over 24 hours. Measured losses are 1.9 L from the nasogastric tube and 0.5 L vomited. What infusion rate, in mL/h, is required?
questions.explanation: Maintenance is 25 x 80 = 2000 mL and measured losses are 1900 + 500 = 2400 mL, so the total is 4400 mL. Dividing by 24 h gives about 183 mL/h, an average that is then adjusted to urine output, electrolytes and haemodynamics.

questions.stem: A reducible femoral hernia can safely be left for routine surveillance because strangulation is rare.
questions.explanation: Femoral hernias have a narrow rigid neck and the highest strangulation risk of the common groin hernias. They are therefore repaired promptly, even if reducible.

questions.stem: Describe the pathophysiology and complications of a strangulated hernia and explain why repair is urgent.
markingGuide: Narrow neck traps bowel; venous outflow obstructed first, causing oedema
Arterial occlusion follows, leading to ischaemia and necrosis
Obstruction with fluid sequestration and dehydration
Need for bowel resection and possibly stoma
Mortality and morbidity rise with delay, so urgent surgery before infarction
questions.explanation: A tight neck compresses the mesenteric vessels, causing venous congestion, arterial ischaemia and necrosis within hours. Early repair preserves viable bowel and avoids resection, perforation and sepsis.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with colicky pain, vomiting, distension and no flatus has had previous laparotomy. Describe how you would distinguish small- from large-bowel obstruction on examination and plain radiography, and outline initial management and indications for surgery.
markingGuide: Small bowel: early vomiting, central dilated loops, valvulae conniventes crossing the whole width, calibre above 3 cm
Large bowel: late vomiting, marked distension, peripheral colon with haustra, calibre above 6 cm (caecum above 9 cm)
Examine all hernial orifices, scars and rectum
Fluids, electrolytes, nasogastric tube, nil by mouth, catheter
CT to identify cause and exclude strangulation
Surgery for peritonitis, strangulation, closed loop or failure of conservative treatment
questions.explanation: Differentiation rests on pattern of symptoms and the position, calibre and mucosal pattern of dilated bowel. Management is resuscitation with decompression and cross-sectional imaging, with surgery for complications.
